Author: @anotherhuman33
Content:
During communist era in Czechoslovakia drugs were almost non existing. If people wanted to get high they would drink or take prescription pills. Borders were closed and tightly controlled, also authorities would go after users as the communist regime wouldn't have allowed western decadent lifestyle. 

In the 70s there was a subculture mainly in big cities who were experimenting with drugs such as codeine or other prescriptions. Someone found in a library step by step guide in an old german book on how to synthesise meth or pervitin as it was called. It was a small group of people who started making it in their homes and using. It became popular due to its potency, it was relatively easy to produce and as I mentioned due to a lack of illegal drugs until 90s, pervitin became very popular. Interestingly, until 90s there was no market and the drug was only shared between users. Because officially communist regime claimed drugs didn't exist in Czechoslovakia, users couldn't get any medical help if they fell into addiction, they were also not aware of the dangers due to lack of information about pervitin. 

Coincidental discovery of the recipe paired with Czech "do it yourself" attitude are some of the reasons why Czechia is Europe's leader in meth production.

Author: @SoldatX
Content:
From 2020 during the pandemic up until October 06, 2024, I've smoked good ole' regular cigarettes. I never tried any hard drug in my life, because from a very young age, my parents conditioned me to avoid such drugs like it's a life or death thing. They emphasized, repeatedly, to never ever touch heroin, conaine, or any kind of drug, but around 2020 I started smoking cigarettes. 

My story and journey with addiction has many similaritilies to what these people were saying. Your life becomes cenetered around the substance. It's all you think about, it's all you do, it's all you feel, your life becomes a sequences of a few-seconds highs in-between each of which is just periods of loneliness, boredom, and an unwavering feeling of incompetence. 

I used to wake up, smoke a cigarette, start working from home or go to the office, and smoke a second one, go for a break, smoke a third, go for lunch, smoke, another break after lunch, smoke, get off work, smoke, come back home, smoke, 1-2 hours later, smoke, and finally go to sleep, but smoke first. I'd be hanging out with friends, and I'm just thinking about my next hit, I'm working, and I'm thinking about my next hit, and I'm doing my hobbies, and all I think is how I'll light up my next cig, fuck, I'll be at a wedding, and I'm anticipating when I'm allowed to leave to smoke. 

It was a fucking nightmare. I realized by the end of 2023 that my life has become unsustainable. I can't have meaning in anything I do, cigarettes pretty much defined my reality. This was the path to quit. 

On October 06, 2024, I transferred all my money and all my funds to an offshore bank account, this is good, they are long-term savings I've been planning on having and it takes 2-3 days for transfers to arrive. So that means, 2-3 days to send, it arrives, and 2-3 days to send back IF I need the money. I bought groceries for the next week or so, and I start my quitting journey. It was fucking awful. 

The first day I slept for more than 15 hours, second day was the same, 3rd day I felt energetic and overall better, 4th day my money arrived in the bank account, didn't touch it, kept going, after week 1 things become easier, week 2 you start feeling really energetic and ready to take on life, week 3 your sleep adjusts, and week 4 you start really feeling the effects of liberating yourself from smoking. 

I'm 1 year and 1 month clean, and my lungs have never been cleaner. My sleep is only fucked up because I spend night coding and playing videogames, they're probelmatic, but it's my choice that I do this, and I derive so much pleasure and value out of them, unlike cigarettes where they just take and give nothing back.

Author: @sephirotic87
Content:
I work professionally with substance abuse disorders and I got a little disappointed with a somewhat shallow bio-social view of the problem of addiction. While it is true that meth is a drug with particularly high risk of addiction due to its neurochemical dynamics and potency, genetics and most importantly, social vulnerabilities are the most crucial factors that lead to a downhill addiction spiral. You can see that the interviewed cases in the video had previous struggles in life which are the highest prediction to risk for drug dependency. 
Also, people that are vulnerable to dependency often don't stick with one drug, they may swap from one substance to another depending of availability or financial reasons, which is EXTREMELY common, and only reforces our clinical knowledge about how genetic and social vulnerability is more important than the an individual drug biochemistry. That being said, I was expecting to hear the professionals that work in the field there in Germany saying how it is extremely important for drug treatment to encompass a multi-disciplinary approach in addition to psychiatric and psychoterapy. It is very important to build up a new safe network away from the old habits, people (that part was covered by the social worker) and help find new friends, family, job shelter and motivation for the patient to seek a new life that can be fulfilling without drugs with a variety of healthy habits and treatments. In the end, if your have a well balanced pleasurable life with goals and hope, you won't find empty pleasure given by drugs that meaningful anymore.  Good luck to anyone looking for help in deal with addiction, I have seen many successful cases in my experience when the motivation and conditions I mentioned above could be met. It is indeed possible to get rid to an addiction, be it alcohol, pills, or meth..

Author: @89ji36
Content:
It's comforting to see so many other people sharing their experiences with drugs and addiction here. Both my older sister and I started using prescription opioids when I was 16 shortly after our little sister died. Within a year we were snorting heroin and probably 6 months after that we were injecting. My big sister and I were so embedded in our addictions and the local "scene" that every once in a while I'll still have people remember me as "the brother from those heroin addict siblings". 

I finally made it out of active addiction in 2016. My big sister and I are still as close as ever, but 3 months after I stopped using she overdosed and suffered a brain injury. We're lucky she still understands everything, has her personality intact and can communicate, but she still requires 24/7 nursing care. I've been the main family member caring for her since 2018, and I honestly wouldn't have it any other way. 

No one knows me like she does and no one knows her like I do. I don't trust some random employee in a nursing home to see who she is and remember there's still a person in there. We talk often about how the people who see her now sitting in this heavy, complicated wheelchair with muscles that won't do what she wants would get a kick out of how crazy we both used to be. 

Sometimes I don't feel like either of us is doing "recovery" correctly. You'd think almost 10 years in while seeing how severely an overdose impacted the person I've always trusted and loved most in life would make me never want to see heroin again. I think about it daily, though. My big sister does, too. It's embarrassing to admit. 

We've lost so many friends over the years. We've lost bits and pieces of ourselves too, I think. My only regret is not having been present when my sister overdosed, though. No one around her had naloxone and no one called for help so she went without oxygen for far too long. If I had been there I would have prevented this from happening. I try not to live in that, though, and she constantly tells me not to. 

I hope that no one else out there has experienced this as a result of their addiction, and if you have please know you aren't alone. There's at least one pair of siblings in the US trying to stay sober while grappling with all the devastation addiction leaves behind.

Author: @finnpayton2173
Content:
One of the most bewildering things about my disease is that, in my experience, its severity progresses whether I'm actively using or not. I've relapsed twice, and it's not like I "picked up right where I left off," but more like I never stopped to begin with. During relapse, my use was more frequent and my actions became more dangerous than they'd ever been. I was all of the sudden stealing money from the register at work, something I had never done. I became abusive to my partner and friends, something I had never been. I thought about killing myself all the time, something that had gone away when I was clean. And worst of all? Author: @frankie1989
Content:
Drug addiction sucks!! We all have are reasons for using drugs, my reason for starting drugs was experimentation, wanting to know what they felt like, overtime tho drugs became a tool that I used to avoid growing up, taking responsibility and accountability, to escape my demons, and to avoid putting in the work to make myself a better human being! 

I started using soft drugs at around 13, by the time i left school I was using harder drugs, by the time i was 20 I was using barbiturates, and opiates, which eventually led to me using heroin. The first time I tried heroin it was like I finally found what I’d been looking for, my anxiety and troubles faded away, and I felt a relaxation that is incomparable to anything else. I wanted to feel heroins effects as much as I possibly could, and In that pursuit I ended up losing everything!! My whole driving force became obtaining and using heroin, nothing else and nobody else mattered!!

In my mid to late twenties I moved away from my hometown, my friends that used, and away from my supply, got on a methadone script and stopped using all drugs entirely. And just before I turned 30 I stopped my methadone cold turkey as well, it was brutal, the withdrawal lasted months!! And the post withdrawal seemed to go on forever, it was around a year before i felt somewhat normal again! However I always felt like something was missing, never quite felt myself, it wasn’t long before I stated pursuing drugs recreationally again. at first it was just weed, that turned into cocaine, and then one day I went to score coke with a friend and we ended up scoring crack, it wasn’t the first time Id tried crack, but looking back on that moment with hindsight, the substance wasn’t really that important, I was just searching for something to alter the way I felt, I was just wanting to escape societal pressures, my responsibilities, I just wanted an escape, at first it was just a brief escape, but as an addict that brief escape quickly turns into my sole driving force, before I know it I pursue that altered state of consciousness constantly. Within a few months of scoring that crack I was back to the races, back in the cycle of securing and using drugs being my whole existence, and not really caring about anything else!! My crack addiction lasted for years, I tried to stop again and again without success!! Started getting in trouble with the law again, started fracturing all my relationships, and above all else started to really despise the person in the mirror, and my life in general! To the extent that I didn’t want to be alive anymore! I’d hit rock bottom and couldn’t seem to find a way out!

Today though, im 36 years old and I’m 214 days clean from all drugs. I’ve rekindled my relationships with my family, started taking care of myself, started working out, and found my faith. Im healthier in so many ways today in comparison to 215 days ago. (Although I am 5 stone heavier) My main battle today is the mental battle, my resilience to stay clean is absolute, but when you spend decades hooked on drugs, you have a lot of trauma and emotions to deal with that you have avoided by abusing drugs, you health is seriously impacted, you burn a lot of bridges, your miles behind your peers in the game of life, and your thinking and mentality has been screwed up from years of drug abuse, so It’s not easy getting clean. recovery is a long hard road that’s never ending. But fortunately I came to a point where I finally said enough is enough! I’m at a point in my life now, where I’d rather man up, take accountability, fight my demons, rebuild my life and pursue an existence free from substances!! 

It hasn’t been easy! “But Nothing worth fighting for ever is”

Author: @codetaku7
Content:
I can't even imagine what it must do to a persons brain to take meth during puberty of all times. Puberty is already the most intense experience most people will ever endure (and we generally do a shit job of helping kids with it), drowning the brain in the highest levels of hormones a person will ever experience in their life. The lifetime maximum is how it STARTS, and its practically debilitating. Combine that with a society that practices denial and rejection of reality to cope, and its a rough road. And then you're going to hit that poor struggling brain with a purer hit of dopamine than life ever offers? That's terrifying. And when it comes to meth, how it is being produced is extremely important. There are different processes for manufacturing meth, and they leave behind different impurities that have different consequences especially with extended use. The most popular method being used in large Mexican labs is called P2P and the meth it produces is more destructive than meth produced through other methods as it leaves behind impurities that seem to pretty reliably result in a slide into psychosis. 

Quitting most addictions is usually most successful when you have some other source of pleasure to turn to in order to replace the pleasure lost from the addiction. Methamphetamine, though, breaks the scales. Like your internal gauge of how good you feel, how you appreciate a good thing happening, etc. Quitting it leaves a person for the rest of their life greeting every positive pleasurable experience with "that's nice, but its no meth." Falling in love? Getting married? Having a child? Seeing your childs first steps? All of it just "that's nice, but its no meth." Truly a drug that poisons the human condition on a fundamental level unlike any other drug. And that's for 'clean' meth, not P2P meth that adds in the obliteration of the mind.

For most addictions, they can be overcome through slow (sometimes very slow, over the course of a year or more) tapering, down to microdosing, and eventually the point is reached where a person feels like its simply not worth doing any more. That doesn't really work with meth, though. Your body and brain can 'bounce back' but the pleasure meth generates won't ever be replaced.

Author: @jacksonbauer5199
Content: As an individual who spent 27 years in a love affair with heroin, I can relate to many of the thoughts/feelings/experiences being shared in this piece… I have personally never been drawn to meth or cocaine. I have honestly never had an enjoyable experience with “uppers”/stimulants, but I am fully aware that any/all substances can/do have a wide variety of effects depending upon the user, their body chemistry, life experience(s), etc., so what may be a nightmare experience for one person is a completely euphoric experience for another. There is one thing that nearly all illicit drugs have in common and that is their unequivocally negative impact on the lives of those who use them and on the lives of those in proximity to said user. Regardless of whether it’s heroin or meth or cocaine or whatever, the negative effects are there, just waiting to “blow up” the lives of those within the radius like a bomb whose timer is slowly ticking down to zero… Sadly though, unlike explosive devices in movies or on TV, there is no visible timer accompanying one’s addiction. The “bomb” can trigger at any moment and wading through the aftermath can sometimes be worse than experiencing the initial “blast”. I don’t want to get too deep into my thoughts and/or feelings regarding the causes of the staggeringly high rates of use/addiction we’ve seen over the past 20-25 years, but I will say that warped public perception, blatantly draconic drug laws, government sanctioned misinformation, the ill advised over-correction employed by the US government, DEA, CBP, etc. have all significantly contributed to the issue(s) at hand. There are better options out there, but convincing people who are deeply entrenched in their own views/beliefs that their “understanding” of the issue is, at best, incomplete and at worst, a garbled mess of propaganda, nonsense, lies and science-for-profit drivel is all but impossible. To be clear, I am not condoning drug use of any kind, nor am I suggesting that the drugs themselves aren’t part of the problem. I was merely pointing out that drugs alone are not the entirety of the issue and, with that being the case, it may be beneficial to approach a “solution” with an open mind. Leave your preconceived notions, ego and emotional investments at the door and instead of seeing these people as addicts first and foremost, try viewing them as humans and not allowing the negative connotations of their addiction to shade your perception of them.

Euphoria, that "high" is caused by a complex cocktail of "hedonic" neurotransmitters which feel good, and then dopamine comes in and makes the body remember what felt so good.

If anything, dopamine is an addiction agent.
If you try dopamine analog, it will not make you feel high.

Author: @CL053DC45K37
Content:
The first step to getting off any drugs is the user has to be mentally done. I mean done done. It starts there first or you will never get clean.  I dont know how many people ive seen who said they wanted to get sober and were sincere because they couldn't get their drug off choice but the second they could they relapsed.  

It took me 3 months to finally make my mind up and that I was done done.  I was looking at two choices one was getting sober thr other was taking my life because I didnt really believe I could get sober.  That is why it took me 3 months to figure it out. I finally realized I was done with this way of life. I had already lost everything thing where that was people leaving my life or me selling off everything I owned to get more.  I was hooked on opiates so a different kind of drug but the addiction is the same.  It controlled everything in my life. I never did a ything if I didn't have enough to last me through whatever it was, from taking a walk, to going to work, to going to the store. If I dodnt have enough to last I didnt do it.  For the 4 years I was using I was lucky enough to get them from a doctor until the last year when I got kicked off by my doctor for smoking weed.  That last year was true hell because I never had enough money to get what I normally used so I was using only to not go through withdrawals. There was no more getting high.  I was using to feel normal and this wrecked my mental state because I finally saw myself for the drug addict I was. After my 3 month inner search on what am I going to do i finally said fuck it and used what little I had and prepared for the withdrawals which are terrible comong off opiates. I made it 18 days before I called the advice nurse who told me to get my ass to the er and tell them you want to enter detox which I did. I only made it 6 of the 21 days I was supposed to stay there because the people who ran this detox were using and I got in a big ass argument with them because they were not telling people coming off alcohol to keep their blood sugar up.  So I did and it helped them but they being the people who worked at this detox got all pissy because I was a patient.   The issue was I lived 3 streets away from this detox center so I left and went home then found a medication assisted treatment program that I qualified for because I was a disabled veteran so I got the help for free.  It wasnt just come in get your medicine and leave no ot was a full program with classes to teach you about your addiction, triggers, how to reach out for help, how to rebuild your life, how to find work, how to set yourself up for success in getting and staying sober.  There were classes in the morning and a group session in the afternoon and you had to do both of these to stay in the out patient treatment program.  The had you bring in whatever family you wanted to bring and they talked to them about it, how to help you, and they taught them how addiction works too so it was an amazing program that saved my life.  I am now 13 years sober and havent used, thought abiut using, or relapsed thanks to this program.

Author: @davekennedy6315
Content:
There is NO physical dependence on Meth/Amphetamines, Cocaine, Crack, Ecstasy! It's a MENTAL not PHYSICAL addiction! I have been addicted over the years to Alcohol (not quite to the point of withdrawal luckily!) Cannabis, Speed/Amphetamines, Ecstasy, Cocaine, Crack and Heroin. I was doing Amphetamines daily for several years verging into psychosis at times. When I stopped as they explained on this documentary I felt ultra tired, utterly without energy, depressed and dull with affected sleep and appetite (rebounds on both) But that is NOT withdrawal, the human body doesn't get physically addicted to uppers. 
Mental addictions (uppers, sex, gambling) are a nightmare to deal with but physical addictions (Opioids, Benzodiazepines, Alcohol) are a literal living Hell in comparison. If you don't do Speed/Meth/Crack one day you will be tired, depressed, angry but your body isn't physically craving the drug. Physical addiction you need that drug EVERY SINGLE DAY without fail or you will feel like you are DYING! I'm fact you CAN and people DO die from withdrawal every day, especially Alcohol and Benzos! There is a collosal difference between feeling tired from not doing Meth to blood pressure dropping, heart issues, strokes, seizures from not taking a physically addictive drug!
So I had addictions with EVERY drug I ever did but only truly knew I'd lost all control with Heroin. You realise that you have no control, the drug is now boss when you HAVE to do that drug daily just to function. Plus dealing with physical addictions can't be done alone, you HAVE to get professional help!
